entries.note: The 2023 technofeudalism exchange read the same facts about cloud rents as capitalism's end or as its new form, depending on the criterion used. No evidence picks the criterion; it has to be stipulated.

author.basis: Henry Snow, "We're Still Living Under Capitalism, Not 'Techno-Feudalism'", Jacobin, 2023-10-27, https://jacobin.com/2023/10/cloud-capitalism-technofeudalism-serfs-cloud-big-data-yanis-varoufakis — reviews Varoufakis's Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism, which holds that rents replacing profits and monopoly replacing competition mean capitalism has ended; the review reads the same 'cloud capital' as capitalism in a novel form. Same facts, divergent criteria for what counts as capitalism.

entries.note: Open-weight models came within 1.7% of closed models on some benchmarks in 2024, down from 8%. Near-frontier capability is not held by a few firms alone; the forecast now turns on compute, chips, and who deploys.

author.basis: Stanford HAI, The 2025 AI Index Report, published 2025-04-07, https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report (release date confirmed at https://www.infodocket.com/2025/04/07/stanford-hai-publishes-2025-artificial-intelligence-index-report/) — 'Open-weight models are also closing the gap with closed models, reducing the performance difference from 8% to just 1.7% on some benchmarks in a single year.' Narrows the model-capability layer of the claim; compute, chip, cloud and ownership layers untouched.

entries.note: By March 2026 the open-model gap had reopened to 3.3%, and six of the top ten Arena models were closed. Near-frontier models stay available outside a few firms, while the top tier and the investment stay concentrated.

author.basis: Stanford HAI, The 2026 AI Index Report, Technical Performance chapter, https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance — 'As of March 2026, the top closed model leads the top open model by 3.3%, up from 0.5% in August 2024. Six of the top ten models on the Arena Leaderboard are now closed.' Date from HAI's 'Inside the AI Index: 12 Takeaways from the 2026 Report', 2026-04-13, https://hai.stanford.edu/news/inside-the-ai-index-12-takeaways-from-the-2026-report, which also reports $581.7B corporate AI investment in 2025 and that giant models are concentrated within the largest AI companies.

entries.note: Payroll data through June 2026: employment of 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs sits 19% below less-exposed peers, mostly through reduced hiring. That bears on entry, not on how fast displaced workers are re-employed.

author.basis: Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen, 'Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence', Stanford Digital Economy Lab, revised 2026-08-12, https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publications/canaries-in-the-coal-mine/ — ADP payroll data through June 2026; young workers in AI-exposed occupations 19% below where they would be had they kept pace with less-exposed peers; operates 'primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations'; authors call these descriptive, not causal.

entries.note: Yale's September 2026 tracker finds no clear AI-related footprint in U.S. employment or occupational mix. The longitudinal re-employment data the resolution condition asks for does not exist yet.

author.basis: The Budget Lab at Yale, 'Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market', published 2026-07-16, updated 2026-09-15, https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/tracking-impact-ai-labor-market — key takeaways: occupational mix 'not yet changing in ways that clearly align with the introduction of AI'; AI usage measures 'show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment'; synthetic DiD 'does not yet clearly indicate an AI-related labor market footprint'. Aggregate stability, not displaced-worker re-employment tracking.

entries.note: Labor's share kept falling (index 93.4 in Q2 2026), but total employee pay and real consumer spending both kept rising through July 2026. The trigger, labor income falling faster than it is recycled, has not appeared.

author.basis: FRED PRS85006173, Nonfarm Business Sector: Labor Share for All Workers, updated 2026-09-03, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PRS85006173 — Q2 2025 96.723, Q2 2026 93.446 (revised from 93.547; the graph node now carries the revision). FRED PCEC96, Real Personal Consumption Expenditures, updated 2026-08-26, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEC96 — 15,317.1 (Nov 2022) to 16,901.3 (Jul 2026), chained 2017 $bn SAAR. FRED W209RC1 compensation received rose from 13,689.2 (Q4 2022) to 16,307.2 (Jul 2026), $bn SAAR, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/W209RC1.

entries.note: Employee compensation was about 60% of U.S. personal income in July 2026, about the same share as in late 2022. Wages are still the largest channel, and no preregistered threshold for a change in kind has been set.

author.basis: BEA via FRED, updated 2026-08-26: W209RC1 Compensation of Employees, Received, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/W209RC1 — 16,307.2 (Jul 2026); PI Personal Income, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PI — 27,114.8 (Jul 2026); both $bn SAAR. Ratio 60.1% (Jul 2026) vs 60.3% (Q4 2022: 13,689.2 over mean monthly PI 22,714.2). Aggregate, all households; the claim concerns non-owners, which these series do not split out.

entries.note: The 2023 review classifies platform rents differently from Varoufakis. A survival verdict still needs an explicit criterion; the review does not settle how AI will change ownership.

author.basis: Correction adds the checked evidence node. Henry Snow, Jacobin, 2023-10-27: https://jacobin.com/2023/10/cloud-capitalism-technofeudalism-serfs-cloud-big-data-yanis-varoufakis. Only the accessible introduction and standfirst were reviewed.

entries.note: The 2025 AI Index records an open-weight performance gap of 1.7% on selected benchmarks, down from 8%. This narrows a capability claim, not the claims about ownership, compute or deployment.

author.basis: Correction links the checked 2025 report: https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report. Its release date is confirmed by Stanford: https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-index-2025-state-of-ai-in-10-charts. Benchmark performance is not market concentration.

entries.note: In March 2026, the top closed model led the top open model by 3.3% on Arena, with six closed models in the top ten. This qualifies the capability picture without measuring ownership or downstream market entry.

author.basis: Correction links the checked Arena snapshot: https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance. Report release: https://hai.stanford.edu/news/inside-the-ai-index-12-takeaways-from-the-2026-report. The 2025 selected-benchmark figure is not a like-for-like comparison.

entries.note: Young workers in exposed occupations were 19% below the employment path implied by less-exposed peers through June 2026, mainly through lower hiring. This descriptive comparison does not measure displaced workers' re-employment.

author.basis: Corrects the earlier note's level-comparison shorthand and adds the checked node. Stanford working paper, revised 2026-08-12: https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/canaries-in-the-coal-mine-six-facts-about-the-recent-employment-effects-of-artificial-intelligence/. The gap attenuates with education controls and is not a causal estimate.

entries.note: Yale's October tracker finds no clear aggregate AI labor-market footprint. These analyses do not measure displaced workers' re-employment and leave the reallocation forecast open.

author.basis: Updates the September source snapshot and links the checked evidence. The Budget Lab, updated 2026-10-14: https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/tracking-impact-ai-labor-market. An undetected aggregate association does not establish that displacement is absent.

entries.note: The labor-share index was 93.446 in Q2 2026, while real consumption rose from July to August. These aggregates do not establish whether income recycling can absorb future losses of labor income.

author.basis: Updates the data vintage and limits the inference. FRED PRS85006173, updated 2026-09-03: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PRS85006173. PCEC96, updated 2026-09-30: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEC96, July 16,862.5 and August 16,955.3, chained 2017 dollars in billions, SAAR. Consumption alone does not measure the recycling trigger.

entries.note: Employee compensation was 59.7% of personal income in August 2026. This aggregate includes benefits and owners of capital, so it does not directly test whether wages remain the main channel for non-owners.

author.basis: Updates the data vintage and limits the inference. FRED releases updated 2026-09-30: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/W209RC1, August 16,485.6; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PI, August 27,626.9, both dollars in billions, SAAR. Argumend calculation: 16,485.6 / 27,626.9 * 100 = 59.6723%, rounded to 59.7%.
